How Durable Agent Runtimes Handle Retries

When an AI agent crashes, gets disconnected, or has to wait days for approval, durable runtimes keep every step of progress safe — and retry without repeating work.

Without durable execution, AI agents lose all progress the moment something goes wrong — a dropped connection, a crashed process, or a slow human reviewer. Durable runtimes fix this by writing checkpoints after each meaningful step, then replaying from the last safe point whenever something fails. Crucially, they also make retries safe: completed work like sending an email or charging a card is never duplicated. The result is an agent that can pause for hours, recover from outages, and survive being killed mid-task without missing a beat.

The Problem with Ephemeral Agent Runs

A normal agent run lives only as long as the process hosting it. The agent reads a user request, kicks off a long research task, calls several tools, and slowly builds up an answer — all while holding its state in memory.

The moment reality intrudes, that state is gone. A WebSocket drops because the user's VPN reconnects, the server running the agent restarts, or the user simply closes their laptop mid-task. The searches that already returned, the documents already read, the partial draft already assembled — all of it disappears [1][5].

This is why demos look smooth and production agents fall over. Demo environments are stable connections with attentive operators watching for thirty-second runs; production agents eventually face network blips, rate limits, crashed processes, and human pauses that last hours or days [1]. As Restate's team puts it, every tool call is a remote hop, every user interaction is a pause, and every retry risks doing the same work twice — agents inherit every failure mode of distributed systems [5].

Checkpoints: Saving Progress at Safe Points

The fix is to write down progress as the agent goes. After each meaningful step — a tool call, an LLM turn, an action that mutates the outside world — the runtime writes a small record describing what just happened and what is needed to continue [1][2].

Microsoft's Durable Task framework calls this 'automatically checkpoint progress and resume from where you left off,' persisting state so the developer doesn't have to manage it by hand [3]. Workflow engines like Temporal, Restate, Inngest, Hatchet, DBOS, Cloudflare Workflows, AWS Lambda Durable Functions, and Azure Durable Task expose the same primitive [2]. Agent frameworks such as LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, AutoGen, CrewAI, Dapr Agents, and Microsoft Agent Framework are layering persistence on top of them [2][5].

A good checkpoint captures three things: the inputs that fed the step, the outputs the step produced, and enough context for the next step to know what to do [2][3]. Without those, the runtime has no way to know which tool call already happened — or whether retrying it would be safe.

Replay: Picking Up Where You Left Off

After a crash, the runtime doesn't restart from the beginning — it replays from the latest checkpoint. It reads the journal, sees what already completed, and skips straight to the next open step [1][2].

This is what makes long-running agents practical at all. A research agent that collected ten sources can be killed at minute forty-five and pick up at minute forty-six, without re-doing the searches or burning another round of API quota [1]. A user who closes their laptop on Friday can come back on Monday and the agent picks up where it paused — no lost work, no duplicate fetches.

Replay only works because checkpoints are durable. Restate's engineers note that the durability model is borrowed directly from distributed systems — they built Restate after spending years on Apache Flink's fault-tolerant runtime and Meta's event-log systems, so wrapping a failing step and persisting its inputs and results is a familiar pattern [5]. Azure Durable Task takes it further: the runtime handles distributed coordination on top of checkpointing, so multi-agent runs can recover across processes, not just within a single one [3].

Idempotent Retries: Doing Work Without Repeating It

Checkpoints and replay solve 'where did I leave off.' They do not, by themselves, solve 'won't my retry send the same email twice' — and that is the harder problem.

Durable runtimes make retries safe through a journal of completed actions. Before redriving a step, the runtime checks the journal: if the tool result is already recorded, it returns that recorded result without calling the tool again. If the tool was a real-world side effect — sending an email, charging a card, calling an external API — the agent must have used an idempotency key, so the same retry produces the same outcome rather than two emails [2][5].

This is why Zylos Research draws a sharp line between session memory and durable execution. Saving chat history helps an agent remember; it does not prove which shell command ran, which email was sent, or which approval was granted [2]. Quellix Labs frames the same idea as durable wrappers around each risky step — the runtime tags them so the retry knows exactly where it stands and never repeats a side effect that was already completed [6]. Calling an LLM again is harmless; charging a customer twice is not.

What Mature Durable Runtimes Add on Top

Beyond checkpoints, replay, and idempotent retries, the field is converging on a small set of additional requirements:

  • Versioned prompts and tools. When an agent's instructions or available tools change between runs, the runtime must know which version was in use so a replay does not accidentally apply new logic to old saved outputs [2].
  • Durable human approvals. When an agent pauses for a human reviewer, the runtime needs to hold that pause for hours or days and resume cleanly when the answer arrives [2][6].
  • Recovery testing. Production-grade systems intentionally crash the runtime at the worst possible moments — mid-tool-call, mid-approval, mid-pause — to prove recovery actually works [2].
  • Multi-tenant isolation. When many users share one runtime, each agent's checkpoints and journals must be strictly isolated so one user's failed run cannot leak into another's [4].
  • Observability. Teams need to see what step an agent is on, what it has already done, and what it is waiting for — especially when a retry or pause lasts longer than expected [4][6].
